sourceCase: United States v. Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. & Ticketmaster L.L.C.
lessonTitle: When a Customer Calls Your Fee Structure a Problem, Listen Fast
situation: On August 22–23, 2022, Live Nation CEO Michael Rapino and several colleagues exchanged messages about a fee dispute tied to Harry Styles tour dates. A business manager — referred to as 'her' — had flagged two specific complaints: fees charged on both the inside and outside of a ticket transaction, and taxes applied to a percentage-based fee. Rapino's direct question was simple: 'what will we say' when asked about two service charges on 50 dates?
insight: Rapino's first move isn't to defend the fees — it's to ask how much they add up to. That's a containment reflex: understand the magnitude before you message. Marcus's follow-up — 'Danger, will robinson... Hopefully this stays contained to Harry' — shows the real fear isn't this one client, it's contagion. Irving (presumably a manager or industry figure, context unclear) already thinks the company 'makes too much money.' One vocal complaint on a high-profile tour could harden that view across the industry. **The hidden strategic logic is protecting pricing power.** Marcus then offers the business justification: inside fees fund one organizational layer, outside fees fund another. That's a **cost-allocation defense** — legitimate or not, it exists in writing. The problem is that it hadn't been communicated to the client before the dispute.
application: If your product has multiple fees — even structurally justified ones — write one plain sentence explaining each before a customer sees their invoice. Don't wait for a complaint to build your rationale. Rapino had to ask 'what will we say' in real time, on a major tour. You want that answer drafted and rehearsed before you're in the spotlight.
pullQuote: The moment a client's manager whispers 'double dipping,' you have minutes to build a clear answer — or you have a narrative crisis.
leadershipTraits: tracks reputational spread, not just individual disputes
reads early warning signs in client complaints
